record.paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
record.original_question: Can a single peer-to-peer system provide fine-grained, user-controlled tuning of the tradeoff between autonomy and efficiency, so that different documents or use cases within the same deployment can choose different storage and search constraints without forcing users to move between separate systems?

evidence.quote: Another interesting area of research is providing fine-granularity tuning of the tradeoff between autonomy and efficiency within a single system.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a data-sharing peer-to-peer system modeled as a collection of nodes (peers), each storing a set of documents and participating in lookup/search protocols. Define peer autonomy as the degree of control a peer has over (i) which documents it stores locally, (ii) which queries it forwards or answers, and (iii) which neighbors it maintains in the overlay. Define efficiency as the expected cost (in messages, latency, or bandwidth) for successfully locating and retrieving a document. Existing designs typically fix a single point on the autonomy–efficiency tradeoff for the whole deployment: structured systems (e.g., distributed hash tables) achieve high efficiency at the cost of dictating document placement and routing, while unstructured systems preserve autonomy but incur higher search cost.

Problem. Design a single peer-to-peer protocol with an explicit tunable parameter (or family of parameters) θ, ranging continuously between a high-autonomy regime and a high-efficiency regime, such that:

1. Each document d (or each user/use case) in the system may independently select its own value θ(d), specifying the storage placement constraints, replication policy, and search strategy used for that document.
2. The system simultaneously supports documents with different choices of θ(d) within the same overlay, without partitioning the peers into separate subsystems.
3. For each choice of θ, prove quantitative bounds on (a) the autonomy granted to peers regarding documents tagged with θ, and (b) the expected search and storage cost, showing that varying θ smoothly interpolates between the autonomy and efficiency extremes.

Either construct such a protocol with provable interpolation guarantees, or prove that no protocol satisfying (1)–(3) can exist subject to a stated formal model of autonomy and efficiency.
artifact.status_search_result: No definitive resolution was located. The question of providing fine-grained, per-document tuning of the autonomy–efficiency tradeoff within a single peer-to-peer overlay remains a design challenge in the P2P literature; various hybrid systems exist but no single protocol with provable continuous interpolation guarantees of the kind requested appears to have been established.
